---
title: "Kriging Metamodeling"
format: html
---

Kriging (Gaussian Process regression) is one of the candidate **expectation models** in `digiqual`. It competes with polynomials of degree 1–10 to describe how the mean signal response changes with the inputs. This page explains exactly how the Kriging candidate is built, how it is chosen (or not), how it feeds the PoD calculation, and where it can mislead you.

## Where each piece comes from

`digiqual` follows two papers and the toolbox they used. Each design choice on this page carries a tag showing its source:

| Tag | Source |
|:---|:---|
| [M25]{.src .src-m25} | Malkiel, Croxford & Wilcox (2025). *A generalized method for the reliability assessment of safety–critical inspection.* Proc. R. Soc. A 481: 20240654. [doi:10.1098/rspa.2024.0654](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.2024.0654). Includes its MATLAB reference code. |
| [M26]{.src .src-m26} | Malkiel, Croxford & Wilcox (2026). *A comprehensive investigation of flexible and multi-dimensional simulation-based PoD analysis.* NDT&E Int. 159: 103596. [doi:10.1016/j.ndteint.2025.103596](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ndteint.2025.103596). |
| [UQLab]{.src .src-uqlab} | A default of the UQLab Kriging module (v2.1). Both papers built their Kriging models with UQLab and its default settings, so these choices are inherited rather than stated in the papers. |
| [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} | A deliberate deviation from the references. Each one is justified in [Deviations from the references](#deviations). |

The roles of the two papers differ:

- **[M25]{.src .src-m25} supplies the overall framework.** It covers the candidate pool, 10-fold cross-validation, the kernel-smoothed variance model, distribution inference and bootstrap confidence bounds. In that paper Kriging is one candidate in the pool (its Fig. 5).
- **[M26]{.src .src-m26} supplies the Kriging-specific machinery.** It covers the GP formulation, choosing the correlation function by leave-one-out (LOO) error, and checking the Kriging uncertainty with standardised LOO residuals.

The full map of what comes from where:

| Element | Source | In `digiqual` |
|:---|:---|:---|
| GP prior, anisotropic correlation | [M26]{.src .src-m26} Eq. 2–5 | One length scale per input |
| Correlation families | [M26]{.src .src-m26} §4.3.1 | Exponential, Matérn 3/2, Matérn 5/2, Gaussian. UQLab's "linear" is omitted [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} |
| Input standardisation | [UQLab]{.src .src-uqlab} `Scaling = true` | $u = (x - \bar{x})/s_x$ per input |
| Length-scale start / lower bound | [UQLab]{.src .src-uqlab} | 1 and $10^{-3}$, in standardised units |
| Length-scale upper bound | [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} | $10^{3}$ (UQLab uses 10) |
| Learned nugget (noise) $\tau^2$ | [M25]{.src .src-m25} reference code (`SigmaNSQ = 'auto'`) | `WhiteKernel`, estimated with the other hyperparameters |
| Hyperparameters by maximum likelihood | [M26]{.src .src-m26} §2.1.2 | Yes. Note that UQLab's own default is LOO-CV estimation |
| Optimiser | [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} (UQLab uses a hybrid genetic algorithm) | L-BFGS-B with 10 random restarts |
| Trend | [M26]{.src .src-m26}: ordinary Kriging (constant estimated by GLS) | Sample mean of $y$ (`normalize_y`) [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} |
| Kernel choice by LOO error | [M26]{.src .src-m26} Eq. 10–14 | Yes |
| 10-fold CV against polynomials | [M25]{.src .src-m25} Eq. 2.7–2.8 | Yes, for the chosen kernel |
| Choosing the simplest near-best model | [M25]{.src .src-m25} §4b(i) | One-standard-error rule [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} |
| Standardised LOO residuals, $\gamma$ | [M26]{.src .src-m26} Eq. 19, §2.2.5.2 | Reported as a diagnostic. Not applied to the PoD [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} |
| Variance model residuals | [M25]{.src .src-m25} Eq. 2.9 (in-sample) | LOO residuals for Kriging [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} |
| Bootstrap bounds | [M25]{.src .src-m25} §2i | Yes, with frozen Kriging hyperparameters [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} |
| Kriging only when $N \le 1000$ | [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} | Above that, only polynomials are fitted |


## 1. The Kriging model

### 1.1 Prior

Kriging treats the response $y = \mathcal{M}(\mathbf{x})$ as one realisation of a Gaussian Process [M26]{.src .src-m26} (Eq. 2–3):

$$
\mathcal{M}^K(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{j=1}^{P} \beta_j f_j(\mathbf{x}) + Z(\mathbf{x}),
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}\!\left[Z(\mathbf{x}), Z(\mathbf{x}')\right] = \sigma^2 R(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}'; \boldsymbol{\theta})
$$

The first term is the trend, $\sigma^2$ is the process variance and $R$ is a correlation function controlled by the length scales $\boldsymbol{\theta}$. [M26]{.src .src-m26} uses *ordinary* Kriging, where the trend is one unknown constant $\beta_0$.

**In digiqual.** The response is standardised, $\tilde{y} = (y - \bar{y})/s_y$, and a zero-mean GP is fitted to $\tilde{y}$. This is *simple* Kriging with the trend fixed at the sample mean $\bar{y}$ [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual}, because scikit-learn's Gaussian Process has no estimated trend. Near the data the two are practically identical. Far from the data the prediction returns to $\bar{y}$ rather than to the GLS estimate $\hat\beta_0$ (Eq. 6 of [M26]{.src .src-m26}). For a constant trend these are usually close.

### 1.2 Distance and correlation functions

Each input is first standardised with the mean and standard deviation of the training data [UQLab]{.src .src-uqlab}:

$$ u_j = \frac{x_j - \bar{x}_j}{s_{x_j}} $$

The correlation then depends on an anisotropic distance with one length scale per input [M26]{.src .src-m26} (Eq. 5; UQLab `Corr.Type = 'Ellipsoidal'`):

$$ d(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{u}') = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \left( \frac{u_j - u_j'}{\theta_j} \right)^2 } $$

Because $\mathbf{u}$ is dimensionless, every $\theta_j$ is measured **in standard deviations of input $j$**. A length scale of 1 means the correlation decays over about one standard deviation of that input. That holds whether the input was recorded in metres, millimetres or degrees.

The four candidate correlation functions [M26]{.src .src-m26} (§4.3.1) are:

| Name in digiqual | $R(d)$ | Smoothness of the fitted surface |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `Exponential (Matern 1/2)` | $\exp(-d)$ | Continuous, not differentiable |
| `Matern 3/2` | $\left(1 + \sqrt{3}\,d\right)\exp\!\left(-\sqrt{3}\,d\right)$ | Once differentiable |
| `Matern 5/2` | $\left(1 + \sqrt{5}\,d + \tfrac{5}{3}d^2\right)\exp\!\left(-\sqrt{5}\,d\right)$ | Twice differentiable |
| `Gaussian (RBF)` | $\exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}d^2\right)$ | Infinitely differentiable |

[M26]{.src .src-m26} also tried UQLab's "linear" correlation. `digiqual` omits it [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} because scikit-learn does not provide it, and in [M26]{.src .src-m26} the Matérn functions consistently beat it.

### 1.3 Noise (nugget)

[M26]{.src .src-m26} studies *deterministic* simulations, where the same inputs always give the same output, so its Kriging model interpolates every training point exactly. `digiqual` is used on data where that is often false. Any influential input you did not include (crack roughness, shape, a random noise realisation) shows up as scatter. Following the [M25]{.src .src-m25} reference code (UQLab option `Regression.SigmaNSQ = 'auto'`), every candidate therefore includes a learned white-noise variance $\tau^2$:

$$ \mathbf{K}_{ij} = \sigma^2 R(\mathbf{u}_i, \mathbf{u}_j; \boldsymbol{\theta}) + \tau^2 \delta_{ij} $$

When the data really are deterministic, maximum likelihood drives $\tau^2$ towards its lower bound and the model reverts to the interpolating Kriging of [M26]{.src .src-m26}.

::: {.callout-important}
## Why the noise must be learned

If $\tau^2$ is fixed below the true scatter variance, the likelihood "explains" the scatter by shrinking a length scale until the surface threads through individual points. This usually happens to a weakly influential input. The result:

- an excellent in-sample fit but a poor leave-one-out fit;
- slices at a fixed value of that input that sag back towards $\bar{y}$ between data points;
- unstable bootstrap refits, which fail the convergence check.

With $\tau^2$ learned, the scatter is attributed to noise and the length scales stay physically sensible. Inputs with no influence get length scales far longer than their range.
:::

### 1.4 Estimating the hyperparameters

For a given correlation function, the hyperparameters $(\sigma^2, \boldsymbol{\theta}, \tau^2)$ are chosen by maximising the log-likelihood of the standardised training responses [M26]{.src .src-m26} (§2.1.2):

$$
\log L = -\tfrac{1}{2}\,\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \tilde{\mathbf{y}} - \tfrac{1}{2}\log\lvert\mathbf{K}\rvert - \tfrac{m}{2}\log 2\pi
$$

In the noise-free ordinary-Kriging case of [M26]{.src .src-m26}, $\beta_0$ and $\sigma^2$ have closed forms (Eq. 6–7), leaving only $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ to optimise numerically:

$$
\hat{\beta} = \left(\mathbf{F}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{F}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{F}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{y},
\qquad
\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{m}\left(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{F}\hat{\beta}\right)^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{R}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{F}\hat{\beta}\right)
$$

With a nugget, `digiqual` optimises $\sigma^2$, $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ and $\tau^2$ together, in log space, with L-BFGS-B started from the default values and then from 10 random points inside the bounds [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual}. UQLab uses a hybrid genetic algorithm instead.

::: {.callout-note}
## Paper vs toolbox
[M26]{.src .src-m26} states that the hyperparameters come from the log-likelihood. UQLab's *default* estimation method is in fact leave-one-out cross-validation (`EstimMethod = 'CV'`), and the [M25]{.src .src-m25} reference code does not override it. `digiqual` follows the paper's description (maximum likelihood).
:::

| Hyperparameter | Initial value | Bounds | Units | Source |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Length scale $\theta_j$ | 1 | $[10^{-3},\,10^{3}]$ | std. devs of input $j$ | start and lower bound [UQLab]{.src .src-uqlab}; upper bound [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} |
| Process variance $\sigma^2$ | 1 | $[10^{-5},\,10^{6}]$ | $\text{var}(y)$ | [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} |
| Noise variance $\tau^2$ | 0.1 | $[10^{-8},\,10]$ | $\text{var}(y)$ | [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual} |
| Numerical jitter | $10^{-10}$ | fixed | $\text{var}(y)$ | [UQLab]{.src .src-uqlab} (`Corr.Nugget`) |

UQLab caps the length scale at 10. `digiqual` allows up to $10^{3}$ so that an input with no influence can become effectively flat instead of sitting on the bound.

### 1.5 Predicting

Conditioning the prior on the data gives the posterior mean and variance at a new point $\mathbf{x}_0$. In the standardised units used by `digiqual` (simple Kriging):

$$
\mu(\mathbf{x}_0) = \bar{y} + s_y\, \mathbf{k}_0^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf{y}},
\qquad
s^2(\mathbf{x}_0) = s_y^2\left(\sigma^2 - \mathbf{k}_0^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{k}_0\right)
$$

where $\mathbf{k}_0$ holds the covariances $\sigma^2 R(\mathbf{u}_0, \mathbf{u}_i)$ between the new point and the training points. Eq. 8–9 of [M26]{.src .src-m26} are the ordinary-Kriging versions. They contain one extra variance term for the uncertainty in $\hat\beta$, which only matters far from the data.

Only $\mu(\mathbf{x})$ is used for the PoD in `digiqual`. The spread of the response around it comes from the separate variance model (§4).


## 2. Choosing the kernel and the model

### 2.1 Choosing the correlation function: LOO error {#loo}

Each of the four candidates is fitted once to all the data. Its leave-one-out predictions then come from a single matrix inverse, without refitting [M26]{.src .src-m26} (Eq. 10–13, after Dubrule 1983). Build the augmented matrix

$$
\mathbf{S} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{K} & \mathbf{F} \\ \mathbf{F}^\mathsf{T} & 0 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{1},
\qquad \mathbf{B} = \left(\mathbf{S}^{-1}\right)_{1:m,\,1:m}
$$

Then the prediction for point $i$ made from all the *other* points, and its variance, are

$$
\mu_{\hat{Y}_{-i}} = -\sum_{j \ne i} \frac{B_{ij}}{B_{ii}}\, y_j,
\qquad
\sigma^2_{\hat{Y}_{-i}} = \frac{1}{B_{ii}}
$$

As in [M26]{.src .src-m26}, the hyperparameters are those fitted to the full data and are not re-optimised for each left-out point. Because $\mathbf{K}$ includes $\tau^2$, $\sigma^2_{\hat{Y}_{-i}}$ is the variance of a new *noisy* observation, which is the right scale for comparing with observed residuals. UQLab computes the same quantities in `uq_Kriging_calc_KFold` [UQLab]{.src .src-uqlab}.

::: {.callout-note}
These LOO formulas are the *ordinary*-Kriging ones (the $\mathbf{F}$ row and column re-estimate the constant trend without point $i$), whereas `digiqual`'s predictions use the sample mean (§1.1). The test suite checks that the matrix formula reproduces an explicit ordinary-Kriging refit to machine precision. The gap between the two trend treatments is negligible for LOO purposes.
:::

The kernel with the smallest normalised LOO error is kept [M26]{.src .src-m26} (Eq. 14):

$$ MSE_{LOO} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{\left(y_i - \mu_{\hat{Y}_{-i}}\right)^2}{\operatorname{var}(\mathbf{y})} $$

$MSE_{LOO} = 1$ means the model predicts left-out points no better than the sample mean. The scores of all four kernels are stored on the model as `kernel_loo_scores_`.

### 2.2 Kriging against the polynomials: 10-fold CV

LOO error with fixed hyperparameters is ideal for comparing kernels, but it is not on the same footing as the polynomials' scores. The chosen kernel is therefore also scored by the same **10-fold cross-validation** as every polynomial, with its hyperparameters re-optimised inside each fold [M25]{.src .src-m25} (Eq. 2.7–2.8):

$$
MSE_j = \frac{1}{N_j}\sum_{i \in \text{fold } j}\left(y_i - \hat{f}^{\setminus j}(\mathbf{x}_i)\right)^2,
\qquad
CV_{(10)} = \frac{1}{10}\sum_{j=1}^{10} MSE_j
$$

This is the Kriging bar in the model-selection chart.

### 2.3 Picking the winner: the one-standard-error rule {#winner}

In [M25]{.src .src-m25} (Fig. 5) the 3rd-order polynomial, the 4th and 5th orders and Kriging all had almost the same CV error, and the authors chose the cubic "since it is the simplest one among those with smaller errors". `digiqual` turns that judgement into a fixed rule [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual}:

1. Find the model with the lowest $CV_{(10)}$.
2. Compute its standard error, $SE = \operatorname{std}(MSE_1, \dots, MSE_{10}) / \sqrt{10}$. The [M25]{.src .src-m25} reference code records this quantity.
3. Choose the **simplest** model with $CV_{(10)} \le \min CV + SE$. The complexity order is Polynomial 1, 2, …, 10, then Kriging.

Kriging is therefore chosen only when it is *clearly* better than every polynomial, not when it wins by a margin smaller than the noise in the CV estimate. You can always override the choice with `model_override="kriging"` or `"polynomial"` (and `force_degree`).

**Example.** The true mean response below is quadratic in flaw length, plus a weak linear effect of probe angle. The cubic polynomial has the lowest CV error, but the fold-to-fold spread is large (the outlier lands in one fold), so every model except Poly 1 is within one standard error of it. Poly 2 is the simplest of those, so it is the automatic choice (red bar). In this case that is also the true model.

```{python}
#| label: fig-one-se
#| fig-cap: "Model selection with the one-standard-error rule. The lowest CV error (bold row, red dash-dot line) belongs to Poly 3, but every bar below the dashed min + 1 SE line is statistically indistinguishable from it, so the simplest of those, Poly 2, is selected."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from digiqual.pod import fit_all_robust_mean_models, plot_model_selection

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
N = 100
length = rng.uniform(0.5, 5.0, N)
angle = rng.uniform(-15.0, 15.0, N)
y = 2.0 * length - 0.3 * length**2 + 0.05 * angle + rng.normal(0, 0.3, N)
y[10] += 3.5  # one outlier

models, cv_scores, winner = fit_all_robust_mean_models(np.column_stack([length, angle]), y)
lowest = min(cv_scores, key=cv_scores.get)
print(f"Lowest CV MSE: {lowest}   Selected (one-SE rule): {winner}")

plot_model_selection(cv_scores, cv_winner_key=winner, cv_se=models[winner].cv_se_)
plt.show()
```

### 2.4 Cost

Kriging needs an $O(N^3)$ factorisation for every likelihood evaluation. One full model build costs 4 kernels × 11 optimiser starts, plus 10 CV folds × 6 starts. Above $N = 1000$ samples Kriging is skipped and only the polynomials are fitted [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual}.


## 3. LOO residual diagnostics and γ {#loo-diagnostics}

To judge whether the Kriging uncertainty estimate can be trusted, [M26]{.src .src-m26} (Eq. 19) standardises each LOO error by its predicted standard deviation:

$$ e_i = \frac{y_i - \mu_{\hat{Y}_{-i}}}{\sigma_{\hat{Y}_{-i}}} $$

If the model's uncertainty is right, the $e_i$ behave roughly like draws from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$. Values outside $[-3, 3]$ flag regions where the model is over-confident. [M26]{.src .src-m26} (§2.2.5.2) defines the factor

$$ \gamma = \max\left(1,\; \frac{\max_i |e_i|}{3}\right) $$

and **multiplies the Kriging interpolation standard deviation by $\gamma$**, which puts the worst residual exactly on the $\pm 3$ line (Fig. 10b of that paper). It then draws posterior GP sample paths with this inflated uncertainty to build a conservative 95 % *bound* on the PoD. The PoD curve itself does not change.

**In digiqual, $\gamma$ is a diagnostic only** [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual}. It is stored as `outlier_scale_factor_` and shown in the Kriging diagnostics plot, where the green crosses are $e_i/\gamma$, as on Fig. 10b's right-hand axis. It is not applied to the PoD, for three reasons:

1. `digiqual` builds its PoD bounds by the [M25]{.src .src-m25} bootstrap, not by GP sample paths, so there is no interpolation-uncertainty term for $\gamma$ to scale.
2. Applying $\gamma$ to the *response scatter* instead would change the PoD curve itself, which [M26]{.src .src-m26} never does. Wider scatter also *raises* the PoD wherever the mean response is below the threshold, so that change is not conservative for small flaws.
3. The nugget $\tau^2$ is one value for the whole input space. When the real scatter varies with flaw size, LOO residuals in high-scatter regions exceed 3 simply because of that. The variance model (§4) already handles this heteroscedasticity, so inflating by $\gamma$ as well would count it twice.

A large $\gamma$ is still worth acting on: look for a missing input, a transformation (e.g. $\log a$), more samples, or a polynomial instead. GP-sample-path bounds in the style of [M26]{.src .src-m26} are a possible future addition.


## 4. Variance model and bootstrap with Kriging

**Variance model.** The scatter around the mean is modelled by the Gaussian kernel smoother of [M25]{.src .src-m25} (Eq. 2.9–2.11), applied to squared residuals. For polynomials those residuals are the usual in-sample ones. For Kriging they are the **LOO residuals** $y_i - \mu_{\hat{Y}_{-i}}$ [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual}. A Kriging model with a learned nugget still bends towards each training point, so its in-sample residuals understate the scatter. That would give too narrow a response distribution and a PoD curve that is too steep. LOO residuals measure how far an observation falls from a prediction that did not use it. The same residuals are used to infer the error distribution ([M25]{.src .src-m25} §2f).

**Bootstrap.** [M25]{.src .src-m25} (§2i) refits the chosen model to each resample of the data, keeping the model type and distribution family fixed. For Kriging, `digiqual` also keeps the hyperparameters ($\sigma^2$, $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, $\tau^2$) and the input scaling at their full-data values. Only the posterior is recomputed, which keeps 1000 refits fast [digiqual]{.src .src-digiqual}. The resulting interval reflects the sampling variability of the data, but **not** uncertainty in the hyperparameters, so it may be somewhat narrow when the length scales are poorly determined (see the pitfalls below). In each resample the variance-model residuals are again leave-out residuals. All copies of a duplicated point are left out together, using the block form of the LOO formula [UQLab]{.src .src-uqlab}.


## 5. Correlation length and other pitfalls (Kriging vs polynomials)

Polynomials are *global*: every data point influences the whole curve, and the shape is fixed by the degree. Kriging is *local*: a prediction is a weighted blend of nearby observations, and the length scale $\theta$ decides what "nearby" means. That locality is why Kriging can follow features a low-order polynomial smooths over ([M25]{.src .src-m25} Fig. 6). It is also the source of most Kriging failures.

### 5.1 The length scale must be longer than the gap between samples

Away from the data, the correlation with every observation decays to zero and the Kriging mean falls back to the prior mean $\bar{y}$. If $\theta$ is *shorter* than the typical spacing between samples, this happens **between** data points. The surface becomes a row of bumps on a flat sheet at $\bar{y}$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-length-scale
#| fig-cap: "Sparse data (10 points) from a saturating response, fitted with the length scale chosen by maximum likelihood and with a length scale shorter than the sample spacing."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Mean response. The ML length scale gives a smooth fit; the short length scale collapses to the mean between points. Grey: outside the data, Kriging decays slowly towards the mean while the cubic polynomial runs away."
#|   - "The same failure seen in a PoD calculation: with the short length scale the PoD dips between samples."
#| layout-ncol: 1
import warnings
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels import Matern, WhiteKernel, ConstantKernel
from digiqual.pod import fit_all_robust_mean_models, build_fixed_kernel_gpr

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

def truth(a):
    return 1 - np.exp(-a / 1.2)

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
a = np.sort(rng.uniform(0.2, 4.0, 10))
y = truth(a) + rng.normal(0, 0.02, a.size)

models, _, _ = fit_all_robust_mean_models(a, y, max_degree=4, n_folds=5)
krig = models[("Kriging", None)]
poly3 = models[("Polynomial", 3)]

# Same model, but with a length scale of 0.08 standard deviations (~0.08 mm here)
short_kernel = ConstantKernel(1.0) * Matern(length_scale=0.08, nu=2.5) + WhiteKernel(1e-4)
krig_short = build_fixed_kernel_gpr(short_kernel, krig.x_mean_, krig.x_std_).fit(a.reshape(-1, 1), y)

grid = np.linspace(0, 6, 400).reshape(-1, 1)
ls = float(np.atleast_1d(krig.kernel_.k1.k2.length_scale)[0]) * krig.x_std_[0]

fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax1.axvspan(a.max(), 6, color="grey", alpha=0.15, label="Outside the data")
ax1.plot(grid, truth(grid), "k:", label="True mean")
ax1.plot(grid, krig.predict(grid), lw=2, label=f"Kriging, ML length scale ({ls:.1f})")
ax1.plot(grid, krig_short.predict(grid), lw=1.5, label="Kriging, length scale 0.08")
ax1.plot(grid, poly3.predict(grid), "--", label="Polynomial, degree 3")
ax1.axhline(y.mean(), color="grey", lw=0.8)
ax1.text(5.9, y.mean() + 0.03, r"$\bar{y}$", ha="right", color="grey")
ax1.plot(a, y, "ko", ms=5, label="Samples")
ax1.set_ylim(-0.3, 1.4); ax1.set_xlabel("Flaw size a"); ax1.set_ylabel("Response")
ax1.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

fig, ax2 = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
threshold, sd = 0.8, 0.05
for model, label in [(krig, "ML length scale"), (krig_short, "Length scale 0.08")]:
    ax2.plot(grid, 1 - stats.norm.cdf((threshold - model.predict(grid)) / sd), label=label)
ax2.plot(grid, 1 - stats.norm.cdf((threshold - truth(grid)) / sd), "k:", label="True PoD")
ax2.set_xlim(0, a.max()); ax2.set_xlabel("Flaw size a"); ax2.set_ylabel("PoD")
ax2.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Maximum likelihood normally avoids this, as in @fig-length-scale-1, where the fitted length scale is roughly ten times the mean spacing. It goes wrong in three situations:

- **Fixed or under-estimated noise.** This is the callout in §1.3. A length scale collapses onto the scatter.
- **Sparse sampling in one direction.** With $n$ inputs, $N$ samples are only about $N^{1/n}$ per axis. [M26]{.src .src-m26} needed 700 points in 4-D, about 5 per axis. The data cannot tell a short length scale apart from a long one along a sparsely sampled direction, so the likelihood is flat there and the estimate is unreliable.
- **Slices through empty regions.** A PoD slice holds unused inputs at their median. If few samples lie near that median for a short-length-scale input, the slice is mostly prior mean.

**What to check.** Compare each fitted length scale (`model.kernel_`, in standard deviations of that input) with the sample spacing along that input. A length scale near its lower bound ($10^{-3}$) is a red flag. A length scale near the upper bound means that input has essentially no effect.

### 5.2 Sparse, uncorrelated (scattered) data

When the signal is weak compared with the scatter, or there are few points, the GP may find no correlation structure at all. The likelihood then puts all the variance in the nugget, pushes $\theta$ to its lower bound and leaves a flat line at $\bar{y}$, so **the trend disappears**.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scattered
#| fig-cap: "15 points with a weak trend buried in scatter. Kriging attributes everything to noise and predicts a constant; its LOO error is above 1 (worse than the mean). A straight line keeps the trend."
b = rng.uniform(0, 4, 15)
z = 0.05 * b + rng.normal(0, 0.3, 15)
m2, s2, w2 = fit_all_robust_mean_models(b, z, max_degree=3, n_folds=5)
k2 = m2[("Kriging", None)]

grid2 = np.linspace(0, 4, 200).reshape(-1, 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.plot(b, z, "ko", ms=5, label="Samples")
ax.plot(grid2, k2.predict(grid2), lw=2, label="Kriging")
ax.plot(grid2, m2[("Polynomial", 1)].predict(grid2), "--", label="Polynomial, degree 1")
ax.set_xlabel("Flaw size a"); ax.set_ylabel("Response"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Fitted kernel: {k2.kernel_}")
print(f"Best kernel LOO error (MSE_LOO): {min(k2.kernel_loo_scores_.values()):.2f}")
print(f"Selected model: {w2}")
```

Polynomials degrade more gracefully here, because a straight line through scattered points still estimates the slope. The model selection usually catches this case: the Kriging CV error is no better than a low-order polynomial's, so the one-SE rule picks the polynomial. Signs to look for are $MSE_{LOO} \gtrsim 1$, a nugget close to 1 (in units of $\text{var}(y)$), and length scales at their lower bound.

### 5.3 Extrapolation

Outside the sampled region a Kriging mean decays back to $\bar{y}$, at a rate set by the length scale (grey region in @fig-length-scale). For a PoD curve that means the mean response at flaw sizes *beyond* the largest simulated flaw drifts towards the average response, so **the PoD can start to fall**. Polynomials fail differently: a cubic or higher-order term can make the mean run away to $\pm\infty$. Neither model should be used outside the sampled range. Keep the PoD evaluation grid inside the range of your simulations.

### 5.4 Other things to be wary of

- **In-sample fit says nothing.** Kriging can pass (almost) through every training point, so in-sample $R^2$ is near 1 for any data. Always judge it by CV or LOO error. The GUI's model-fit diagnostic uses LOO predictions for Kriging for exactly this reason.
- **One length scale for the whole space (stationarity).** A response that rises steeply for small flaws and then saturates has two very different "natural" length scales, and a stationary GP must compromise. Transforming the input (e.g. working in $\log a$, as [M25]{.src .src-m25} §2g recommends) often makes the response closer to stationary.
- **One noise level for the whole space.** The nugget $\tau^2$ is constant. If the real scatter varies strongly, the Kriging surface may be over-smoothed where the scatter is small and under-smoothed where it is large, and the LOO residuals will flag outliers ($\gamma > 1$). The variance model accounts for the varying scatter in the PoD itself.
- **No equation.** A polynomial can be written down and checked by hand. A Kriging model is defined by its training data and hyperparameters, which makes it harder to audit.
- **Cost and size limit.** Fitting is $O(N^3)$, and Kriging is skipped above 1000 samples.
- **The variance smoother is not scaled.** The Kriging inputs are standardised, but the kernel smoother for the variance model still uses Euclidean distance in the raw input units, with a single bandwidth.

### 5.5 Summary: Kriging vs polynomials

| | Polynomial | Kriging |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Shape | Global, fixed by degree | Local, set by length scales |
| Between samples | Smooth by construction | Smooth only if $\theta \gtrsim$ sample spacing |
| Outside the data | Can diverge (high degree) | Decays to $\bar{y}$ |
| Sparse or noisy data | Robust, keeps the trend | May collapse to a constant |
| Sharp local features | Smoothed out (low degree) | Captured if well sampled |
| Many inputs | Number of terms explodes with degree | One length scale per input |
| Scatter in the response | Least-squares fit (Ridge) | Learned nugget $\tau^2$ |
| Interpretability | Explicit equation | No equation |
| Cost | Negligible | $O(N^3)$; $N \le 1000$ |


## Deviations from the references {#deviations}

| Deviation | Reference | Why `digiqual` differs | Expected effect |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Trend fixed at $\bar{y}$ (simple Kriging) | [M26]{.src .src-m26}: GLS-estimated constant | scikit-learn has no estimated trend | Negligible near data; far from data reverts to $\bar{y}$ instead of $\hat\beta_0$ |
| No "linear" correlation family | [M26]{.src .src-m26} §4.3.1 | Not in scikit-learn; Matérn beat it in [M26]{.src .src-m26} | None expected |
| Length-scale upper bound $10^{3}$ | [UQLab]{.src .src-uqlab}: 10 | Lets irrelevant inputs become flat | Fewer length scales stuck on a bound |
| Multi-start L-BFGS-B | [UQLab]{.src .src-uqlab}: hybrid GA | scikit-learn optimiser | Same optimum in well-posed problems |
| ML estimation | [UQLab]{.src .src-uqlab} default: LOO-CV | Follows the [M26]{.src .src-m26} text | — |
| One-SE winner rule | [M25]{.src .src-m25}: qualitative "simplest of the near-best" | A reproducible version of the same idea | Prefers simpler models in near-ties |
| $\gamma$ not applied | [M26]{.src .src-m26}: inflates interpolation std for GP-path bounds | No GP-path bounds in `digiqual`; applying it to scatter would change the PoD curve and double-count heteroscedasticity (§3) | PoD curve and bounds unaffected by $\gamma$ |
| LOO residuals for the variance model | [M25]{.src .src-m25}: in-sample residuals | A nugget GP's in-sample residuals understate the scatter | Wider, more honest scatter for Kriging |
| Frozen hyperparameters in the bootstrap | [M25]{.src .src-m25}: refit each resample | 1000 re-optimisations are too slow | Bounds omit hyperparameter uncertainty |
| Ridge polynomials | [M25]{.src .src-m25}: ordinary least squares | Stabilises high degrees | Slight shrinkage of high-degree terms |
| $N \le 1000$ for Kriging | — | $O(N^3)$ cost | Polynomials only for large data |


## 6. Python example

```{python}
#| label: fig-kriging-results
#| fig-cap: "Standardised LOO residuals for the selected Kriging model."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Distribution of the standardised LOO residuals against N(0, 1)."
#|   - "Residuals against the ±3 outlier threshold. Green crosses are the residuals divided by γ (diagnostic only)."
#| layout-ncol: 1
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from digiqual.pod import fit_all_robust_mean_models, compute_kriging_loo_residuals
from digiqual.plotting import plot_kriging_diagnostics

# 1. Synthetic 2D data: flaw length and probe angle
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
N = 100
length = rng.uniform(0.5, 5.0, N)
angle = rng.uniform(-15.0, 15.0, N)
X = np.column_stack([length, angle])
y = 2.0 * length - 0.3 * length**2 + 0.05 * angle + rng.normal(0, 0.3, N)
y[10] += 3.5  # one outlier

# 2. Fit the candidate pool
models, cv_scores, winner = fit_all_robust_mean_models(X, y)
gpr = models[("Kriging", None)]

print(f"Selected model (one-SE rule): {winner}")
print(f"Kernel LOO errors: { {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in gpr.kernel_loo_scores_.items()} }")
print(f"Chosen kernel: {gpr.best_kernel_name_}")
print(f"Fitted kernel (standardised inputs): {gpr.kernel_}")
print(f"Length scales in input units: {np.atleast_1d(gpr.kernel_.k1.k2.length_scale) * gpr.x_std_}")
print(f"gamma (diagnostic): {gpr.outlier_scale_factor_:.2f}")

# 3. LOO residual diagnostics
loo_means, loo_stds, std_res, gamma = compute_kriging_loo_residuals(gpr, X, y)
fig_hist, ax_hist = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
fig_scatter, ax_scatter = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
plot_kriging_diagnostics(std_res, outlier_scale_factor=gamma, best_kernel_name=gpr.best_kernel_name_,
                         ax=(ax_hist, ax_scatter))
plt.show()
```


## API summary

| Function | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| [`pod.fit_all_robust_mean_models`](../api_reference/pod.fit_all_robust_mean_models.qmd) | Fits the polynomial pool and the Kriging candidate, scores them, and picks the winner. |
| [`pod.select_cv_winner`](../api_reference/pod.select_cv_winner.qmd) | One-standard-error rule. |
| [`pod.build_kriging_candidate_kernels`](../api_reference/pod.build_kriging_candidate_kernels.qmd) | The four candidate kernels, $\sigma^2 R + \tau^2\delta$. |
| [`pod.ScaledGaussianProcessRegressor`](../api_reference/pod.ScaledGaussianProcessRegressor.qmd) | GP with UQLab-style input standardisation. |
| [`pod.build_kriging_gpr`](../api_reference/pod.build_kriging_gpr.qmd) | An unfitted Kriging model with the production settings. |
| [`pod.build_fixed_kernel_gpr`](../api_reference/pod.build_fixed_kernel_gpr.qmd) | A Kriging model with frozen hyperparameters and scaling, for bootstrap refits. |
| [`pod.compute_kriging_loo_residuals`](../api_reference/pod.compute_kriging_loo_residuals.qmd) | LOO means, variances, standardised residuals and $\gamma$ ([M26]{.src .src-m26} Eq. 10–19). |
| [`pod.compute_kriging_group_loo_means`](../api_reference/pod.compute_kriging_group_loo_means.qmd) | Leave-one-group-out means, for resamples with duplicates. |
| [`pod.fit_variance_model`](../api_reference/pod.fit_variance_model.qmd) | Residuals (LOO for Kriging) and bandwidth for the variance model. |
| [`plotting.plot_kriging_diagnostics`](../api_reference/plotting.plot_kriging_diagnostics.qmd) | LOO residual histogram and outlier scatter ([M26]{.src .src-m26} Fig. 10). |
